evidence.section_title: "I have sinned": understanding the role of religion in the experiences of suicide attempters in Ghana
evidence.quote: This qualitative study examined the role played by religion in the experiences of persons who attempted suicide in Ghana.
The study was conducted in Accra, the capital of Ghana.

Data were collected at five hospitals and clinics in Accra. Informants were mostly Christian with only two being Muslim. They were asked to describe what led to the suicide attempt, the act itself and the reaction of those around them. Though a direct question was asked in the course of the interview on how religion featured in their experiences, for most informants, religious reflections and experiences had spontaneously emerged while describing the suicidal experience. The interviews took place within a week of the act and were narrative in nature, a process that allowed informants to refer to the actual concrete events in space and time, suffusing these experiences with meaning and significance. Here, we present emerging themes relating to how informants perceived and understood their suicidal experiences in a religious context. All interviews were conducted by the first author who is a native Ghanaian psychologist.

evidence.section_title: "I have sinned": understanding the role of religion in the experiences of suicide attempters in Ghana
evidence.quote: This qualitative study examined the role played by religion in the experiences of persons who attempted suicide in Ghana. We found that religion provided a broad context within which the informants' experiences could be understood. All informants acknowledged God as owner of life and death. Whereas the majority reacted to the suicidal act in a way that resonates with their religious system and sought for forgiveness from God, a few reacted in opposition to the system and expressed anger and disappointment in God. Implications of our findings for suicide prevention in Ghana are discussed.

Many informants expressed guilt feelings after the suicidal act as illustrated in the following quotes: " … and I was crying because I was feeling so guilty before God. I felt so guilty … after I did that" (woman 3) and "I wish I never did what I did … but it has happened" (woman 4). The act itself was perceived as a sin which makes them consider it as a violation of the basic moral guidelines in their religious system.

In our sample, having acknowledged that they had violated the moral guidelines in their religion not to commit sin, the informants perceived their act as injurious to their personal relationship with God. Seeking forgiveness could thus be seen as an act of restoration of the relationship. Informants taking this path accepted the moral code of their religion, took responsibility, and tried to re-establish a relationship with God by pleading for forgiveness.

Findings revealed that religion provided a context for understanding the experiences of the informants in the study. Generally, informants acknowledged God as owner of life and death. Consequently, no one had the right to tamper with life. Taking one's life then is a moral transgression according to their belief system. van Praag (2009) presented two views of God: as a consoler and as a tyrant. In perceiving God as a consoler, people think of the protective effect of religion. For example, religious commitment and active involvement in religious activities make people feel they belong, are accepted, and appreciated by like-minded people. Also, religion by itself may offer relief and hope in times of stress. However, religion might also affect mental health by undermining rather than improving coping abilities (van Praag, 2009). In such situations, God might be experienced as a threatening and punishing authority, and a tyrant, making religion become a burden and a source of worry (van Praag, 2009). The majority of our informants seemed to perceive God as consoler and they saw their suicide attempt as their own responsibility and a crime against God. Consequently, they experienced guilt and tried to restore the relationship with God by asking for forgiveness. A minority, on the other hand, seemed to understand God as a tyrant as he did not fulfil his promises even though they had fulfilled their religious duties. Consequently, they were disappointed and angry and refused to have anything to do with God. In sum, the informants seemed to have a mental or spiritual contract with God that either they or God broke, leading to specific actions and consequences for them. ... The cognitive dissonance theory (Festinger, 1957) focuses on the degree to which attitudes and behaviours are consistent. It holds that discrepancy between an individual's beliefs and behaviour leads to dissonance which the individual is motivated to resolve. According to Festinger, this can be achieved by either rationalising the situation or taking concrete action to reduce the dissonance. Typically, the informants held the belief that because God owns life no one is supposed to take his/her life. Suicide is therefore perceived as a sin before God. However, overwhelmed by life challenges and perhaps not finding any solace, not even in God, the informants decided to take their lives. This created a discrepancy between their beliefs and behaviour and eventually led to dissonance. The dissonance created then resulted into guilt and regret as well as condemnation of their behaviour. To reduce the dissonance, some informants asked for forgiveness from God while others simply rationalised their behaviour by indicating that they were angry with God for not fulfilling his part of the religious contract. A few men solved the problem by refusing it to be a problem and denouncing themselves as victims. ... In this study, with the feeling of shame and abandonment by God, and in the absence of any form of social support, informants might have felt entrapped and therefore engaged in suicidal behaviour.
